title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution (planned episodes 600, completed 600, model_calls_used 301) produced baseline = 299/300 valid configurations (99.667%) and guarded = 300/300 valid configurations (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.00333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair call corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered power calculation assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40 and a target relative reduction of 50% (mapped to absolute +30 percentage points); the observed near‑ceiling baseline invalidates that planning assumption. We report preregistered design, execution accounting, statistical results, a short post‑hoc sensitivity statement grounded in the archived contingency counts and bootstrap CI, and operational and methodological implications for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. Full run artifacts (execution manifest and analysis artifacts) are archived with the study.

sections.introduction: Automating the translation of high‑level operator intent into device configuration is a promising avenue to accelerate network operations but introduces operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or otherwise unsafe. Recent surveys and system proposals increasingly recommend generate→verify→repair patterns that combine probabilistic generators with deterministic validators or simulators to reduce misconfiguration risk. We implemented a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment that tests a minimal guarded pipeline: one shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), a frozen deterministic validator that performs rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, and up to one automated repair attempt when the validator detects violations. Our core research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Contributions: (1) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment (N=300) with deterministic seed generation and full archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces; (2) an evidence‑grounded analysis showing that the observed near‑ceiling baseline undermined the preregistered power assumptions; (3) operational and methodological recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations (task difficulty calibration, paired sampling semantics, and repair iteration policy choices).
sections.related_work: Prior work demonstrates both promise and risk for LLM‑assisted NetOps. Empirical demonstrations and surveys document that LLMs can synthesize configuration templates from intent but suffer failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that have operational consequences. Cross‑domain studies (medical QA, code generation) show that retrieval augmentation, deterministic verifiers, and repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding; architectural proposals for NetOps recommend deterministic validators as floor‑safety nets and generate→verify→repair pipelines for agentic workflows. However, the literature contains few preregistered A/B experiments that quantify misconfiguration‑rate reductions using a deterministically generated paired test set with a frozen validator plus a bounded automated repair budget. Our work situates itself as a narrowly scoped, artifact‑archived confirmatory test of that minimal pattern and connects observed statistical outcomes to broader recommendations in the literature.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypotheses: The study was preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1). Confirmatory hypotheses were H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces the first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus plain single‑shot generation; and H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly assumed a planning baseline success rate of 0.40 (baseline fail rate 0.60); mapping a 50% relative reduction in fail rate under that assumption corresponded to an increase in pass rate from 40%→70% (absolute +30 percentage points). Design and sampling: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds produced by the frozen task generator. Each seed produced two paired episodes: baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the same sampled candidate validated and, if invalid, subjected to at most one automated repair attempt). The execution contract fixed initial_generation_calls_per_task=1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. Importantly, the run used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (the same sampled LLM candidate was presented to both arms for each pair), which increases within‑pair correlation and reduces the number of discordant pairs available for McNemar‑type inference. Model and runtime: the declared model was gpt-5-mini and the frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter was used as specified in the preregistration. Planned vs actual: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs); execution completed 600 episodes with model_calls_used = 301 and the provider audit recording stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}. Analysis plan: the primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline tested with the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05). Primary analysis reported absolute and relative reductions with 95% CIs; missingness and failed‑call treatments followed preregistered policies. All raw responses, per‑task validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts were archived for reproducibility; readers may consult the archived execution manifest and analysis artifacts for per‑task diagnostics.
sections.results: Execution accounting and artifact summary: planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301, repair calls invoked = 1. Contamination and failure checks: no provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; contamination checks flagged no deterministic exact duplicates among preregistered seeds; no exclusions or replacements were executed. Primary outcomes (archive‑derived): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%); paired contingency counts n11=299, n10=1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01=0, n00=0. Statistical inference: exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference estimate = 0.0033333333. Paired bootstrap (percentile) 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair outcomes and H2: the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1). The Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for repair success with denominator 1 is [0.025, 1.0], reflecting wide uncertainty from the single case. Post‑hoc sensitivity and interpretive quantification: the observed discordant pair count (n10+n01 = 1) imposes a hard limit on resolvable absolute paired difference equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333, matching the point estimate. The observed bootstrap CI upper bound of 0.01 further bounds plausible absolute improvement under the run's sampling semantics. By design the preregistered target absolute change (≈0.30) is orders of magnitude larger than the empirically resolvable difference in this run; hence the observed near‑ceiling baseline invalidates the preregistered power planning and the run has negligible statistical power to detect the preregistered effect size.
sections.discussion: Operational and methodological lessons: (1) Baseline alignment with preregistered effect sizes is essential. Our preregistered power plan assumed baseline pass rate = 0.40 and targeted a 50% relative reduction in fail rate (≈+30 percentage points absolute). The observed baseline (299/300) left virtually no headroom to detect that confirmatory target. Researchers designing confirmatory NetOps tests should calibrate task banks to plausibly produce the baseline failure rates that motivate planned effect sizes. (2) Paired sampling semantics materially affect inferential leverage. Reusing a shared initial candidate per pair (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") increases within‑pair correlation and reduces the number of informative discordant pairs McNemar relies on; independent candidate draws increase discordant‑pair potential but also increase heterogeneity—both options must be prespecified and power‑checked. (3) Repair‑effect estimation requires more initial failures. A single repair success (1/1) demonstrates that the repair mechanism can correct that class of validator‑detected violation, but the wide Clopper–Pearson interval shows that many more initial failures are needed to estimate repair effectiveness precisely. (4) Evaluative regimes for operational readiness should combine: a) harder or adversarial task banks to increase baseline failure counts, b) richer validator fidelity (dynamic emulation in addition to deterministic constraint checks) to measure runtime consequences, c) explicit planning of paired sampling semantics, and d) a repair budget reflecting realistic operational policies (multiple iterative repairs and human‑approval thresholds). (5) Reproducibility and archival practice: our run archives model responses, per‑task validator and repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts. That archival permits post‑hoc sensitivity checks (e.g., alternative missingness treatments) and facilitates follow‑on experiments that intentionally raise task difficulty or alter sampling semantics. Threats to validity: internal validity is affected by the shared‑candidate pairing choice; construct validity is limited because deterministic validator checks do not execute configurations in a live network; external validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, single model family, and single validator implementation.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300) using gpt‑5‑mini and a frozen deterministic validator with ≤1 automated repair iteration, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single permitted automated repair corrected the only observed failure but did not yield a statistically detectable improvement for the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis because the observed baseline invalidated the preregistered power assumptions. We document execution accounting and statistical artifacts, quantify the inferential limits imposed by the observed contingency counts (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01]), and provide concrete recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations that aim to measure practical safety gains for guarded LLM pipelines. Full archived artifacts accompany this manuscript to support reproducibility and method refinement.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.

Sampling semantics (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
